rv.q: Wodehouse’s brilliant turn of phrase and comedic flair is not in doubt, and this unadulterated dramatisation offers the full impact of his articulation and wit.
Harrison delivers each story beautifully, switching character to character at the snap of a finger and bringing each one of them onto the stage for the audience to meet and get to know.
For all its engaging and thoughtful elements, this is, however, a production that outstays its welcome.
For the rest, it feels like inconsequential nonsense that only PG Wodehouse fanatics would truly enjoy.
It is a master class in both performance and direction and set against an extremely attractive design.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a bally good, one‑man delight.
With clever staging and a mesmerising performance, Jeeves Takes Charge is full of laughs from beginning to end.
Jeeves Takes Charge might need some extra help to win the house over and eventually exploit its full potential.
His performance alone is worth the ticket price.
A welcome return then for Wodehouse aficionados and perhaps a useful introduction for newcomers, this lavish production features a remarkable central performance.
Jeeves Takes Charge ultimately becomes an unusual contradiction: an astonishing central performance trapped inside a relatively unsuccessful revival.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a fun, very reverent take on the works of P.G Wodehouse, with a great physical performance from Sam Harrison.
However, the lack of meaningful plot or character arcs means that, despite enjoying the play in the moment, it doesn’t leave much of a lasting impression.
I found the plot difficult to follow amidst the constant stream of text that becomes quickly exhausting, and hard to invest in.
A most charming, amusing and delightful escape from the outside world.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a charming and cleverly staged piece of quintessentially British theatre.
The evening is stretched out thinly, however, and our patience is challenged as we approach the two-hour mark.

cn.t: Sam Harrison's virtuosic one-man performance playing 22 characters earns widespread praise, but critics are divided on whether Wodehouse's genteel humor and thin plotting fully connect with modern audiences.
